newsitem.title: BULGARIA: E. European countries join forces to combat crime.
newsitem.headline: E. European countries join forces to combat crime.

text.p: Police officers from eastern European countries and Germany said on Thursday they would widen cooperation in a bid to crackdown on trans-border organised crime.

At a three-day meeting here, high-ranking police officers from Bulgaria, Romania, the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Germany and Interpol in Austria discussed how to coordinate their efforts in the fight against drug smuggling, car theft and trafficking in people.

"This meeting marks the beginning of an operational and (police) cooperation in the fight against crime, promoting quick exchange of information and experts," Bulgaria's police deputy director Dimitar Moskov told a news conference at the end of the meeting.
The meeting also dealt with problems related to crime in the financial sphere, the theft of intellectual property and racketeering, Moskov said.
Bernhard Falk, vice-president of the Federal and Criminal Office of Germany said that in the last two years the number of stolen cars in Germany has decreased.
"But car theft is still a big problem. About 110,000 cars per year are stolen in Germany and some 60,000 of them disappear," Falk told Reuters.

"We think that a lot of these luxury cars such as Mercedes, BMW, Audi and Porsche have been transported to middle and eastern European countries and from there to the Far East, for example to Japan," he said.
Trafficking in people from eastern European countries willing to emigrate and trafficking in women for sexual exploitation is an increasing type of organised crime, Falk said.

"A lot of young women and girls from Poland, the Czech Republic and Slovakia go to Germany to work as prostitutes and that type of crime is closely connected to other types of crime such as drug abuse and drug trafficking," he said.
Falk said there were several drug-trafficking routes across the Balkans and the classic "Balkan route" via former Yugoslavia had been restored after the end of the war there.
Detlev Rein, advisor to Germany's Interior ministry said that central and eastern European countries, located on a drug transit route, had been used for the illegal storage of drugs.
"These countries...are used as storages for drugs so that smaller quantities can be smuggled to western Europe," Rein told a news conference through an interpreter.
He said the activities of criminal organisations should be "stopped not only on borders but we should act in the countries where their headquarters are based."
